4.1.simple: Krishna says this timeless teaching of yoga is very old: he first gave it to Vivasvan (the sun), who passed it to Manu, who passed it to King Ikshvaku. Wisdom has a long lineage.

4.2.simple: Wise kings handed this teaching down, one to the next, but over a long time it was lost. Even great wisdom fades unless each generation keeps it alive.

4.3.simple: Krishna now shares that same ancient teaching with Arjuna because Arjuna is his devoted friend. Deep truths are often passed on through trust and friendship.

4.4.simple: Arjuna is puzzled: Krishna was born recently, while the sun is ancient, so how could Krishna have taught it first? It is an honest, reasonable question.

4.5.simple: Krishna explains that both he and Arjuna have lived many lives; Krishna remembers them all, while Arjuna does not. Our view of our own story is limited.

4.6.simple: Krishna says that though he is unborn, unchanging and the Lord of all beings, he appears in the world by his own divine power. His coming is a free choice, not a compulsion.

4.7.simple: Whenever goodness declines and wrongdoing grows, Krishna says he appears in the world. It is a promise that the world is never abandoned.

4.8.simple: He comes, age after age, to protect the good, to end destructive wrongdoing, and to re-establish dharma (what is right). Goodness always gets renewed support.

4.9.simple: Whoever truly understands the divine nature of Krishna's birth and actions is not reborn after this life, but comes to him. Real understanding brings freedom.

4.10.simple: Many people, freed from clinging, fear and anger, focused on the Divine and taking refuge in it, have been purified by knowledge and reached the Divine. The path is well travelled.

4.11.simple: In whatever way people approach the Divine, the Divine meets them in that same way. Everyone, in their own way, is walking toward the same goal.

4.12.simple: People who want quick success in worldly life worship the gods (forces of nature), and such efforts bring fast results here. Krishna acknowledges this without judging it.

4.13.simple: Krishna says society's four kinds of roles were arranged according to people's qualities and the kind of work they do. Though he set this up, he himself remains unchanged and unattached.

4.14.simple: Actions do not stain Krishna, because he does not crave their results. Anyone who understands this is also freed from the bondage of action.

4.15.simple: Knowing this, seekers of freedom long ago kept doing their work. So Arjuna should act too, in the same spirit as the wise ones before him.

4.16.simple: What is action, and what is inaction? Even wise people get confused here. Krishna offers to explain it, because understanding it sets us free.

4.17.simple: We need to understand right action, wrong action and inaction, because the way action works is subtle. Thoughtfulness matters more than simple rules.

4.18.simple: The wise see stillness within activity and activity within stillness. They can be busy outside yet calm inside, and they notice that avoiding a duty is also a kind of action.

4.19.simple: When someone's efforts are free of selfish craving, and their actions are cleansed by wisdom, the wise call that person truly wise.

4.20.simple: Letting go of attachment to results, always content and not dependent on anything, such a person is not bound even while fully busy. Their inner freedom stays intact.

4.21.simple: Free from greed and grasping hopes, with a steady mind, doing only what the body needs, such a person does no wrong. Simple, uncraving action leaves no stain.

4.22.simple: Content with what comes naturally, beyond the push and pull of opposites, free from envy, and steady in success or failure, such a person acts without being bound.

4.23.simple: For someone free of clinging, with a mind settled in wisdom, who acts as an offering, their actions dissolve without leaving any binding trace.

4.24.simple: For one who sees the Divine everywhere, the offering, the act of offering, the fire and the one who offers are all Brahman (the Divine). Seeing this way, every action becomes sacred.

4.25.simple: Some offer worship to the gods, while others offer their very self into the Divine. Krishna starts to describe the many forms that yajna (offering) can take.

4.26.simple: Some offer their senses into the fire of self-restraint; others offer what they experience through the senses as an offering. Both control and mindful enjoyment can be sacred.

4.27.simple: Others offer all the work of the senses and the life-breath into the fire of self-control, lit by knowledge. Mastering ourselves can itself be an offering.

4.28.simple: Some offer wealth, some their discipline, some their practice of yoga, and some their study and learning. There are many ways to give.

4.29.simple: Some practice breath control, balancing the incoming and outgoing breath, as their offering. Even breathing, done with awareness, can be a spiritual practice.

4.30.simple: Others offer through moderate eating and care for their life-energy. All these people understand the spirit of offering, and it cleanses them.

4.31.simple: Those who enjoy what remains after offering taste something like nectar and reach the eternal. Without a spirit of giving, even this life does not go well, let alone the next.

4.32.simple: All these many kinds of offering are described in the scriptures, and all of them involve action. Understanding this sets you free.

4.33.simple: Offering wisdom is greater than offering material things, because all action finds its fulfilment in true understanding. Knowledge is where every effort leads.

4.34.simple: Learn this wisdom by approaching those who have realized the truth with humility, sincere questions and service. They will share it with you.

4.35.simple: Once you gain this wisdom, you will not be confused like this again, and you will see all beings in yourself and in the Divine. Everything becomes connected.

4.36.simple: Even if you have made more mistakes than anyone, the raft of wisdom can carry you across them all. No one is beyond the reach of understanding.

4.37.simple: Just as a blazing fire turns wood to ash, the fire of knowledge burns away the binding effects of past actions. Wisdom transforms our past.

4.38.simple: Nothing in the world purifies like true knowledge. Someone steady in yoga discovers it within themselves, naturally, in due time.

4.39.simple: A person with sincere faith, dedicated to the path and guiding their senses, gains this wisdom, and with it soon finds the deepest peace.

4.40.simple: Someone who refuses to learn, lacks trust and doubts everything finds no happiness, here or beyond. Endless doubt leaves no ground to stand on.

4.41.simple: One who has offered their actions through yoga, whose doubts are cleared by wisdom, and who is centered in the Self, is not bound by their actions.

4.42.simple: So, Krishna says, cut through the doubt in your heart with the sword of wisdom, take your stand in yoga, and rise up. Clarity leads to courageous action.

lessons.title: Wisdom passed hand to hand
lessons.teaching: Krishna explains that this teaching is ancient, handed down from teacher to student until it was forgotten. He renews it for Arjuna because of their trust and friendship. Timeless wisdom stays alive only when people share it with care.
lessons.keyIdea: Good wisdom survives when we pass it on.

apply.scenario: Your grandmother has a lifetime of wisdom about patience and family, but you rarely ask her about it because you are busy and assume it is old-fashioned.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Skip it; old advice does not apply to modern life.
Spend real time with her, asking and listening, so her wisdom is not lost.
Search the internet instead, since it has all the answers anyway.
Wait until a crisis comes up, then ask her what to do.
apply.why: In 4.2 Krishna notes that wisdom passed down through generations was lost over time, and in 4.3 he renews it through a trusting relationship.

lessons.reflect: What wisdom have I received from someone older that I would like to keep alive?
lessons.practice: Ask an older person today one question about a lesson life has taught them.

lessons.title: Goodness is never abandoned
lessons.teaching: Krishna says that whenever goodness weakens and wrongdoing grows, the Divine steps in to protect the good and renew what is right. This is a message of hope: the world is not left alone. Those who let go of clinging, fear and anger find their way to that same goodness.
lessons.keyIdea: When goodness fades, it is always renewed.

apply.scenario: You read the news and feel the world is getting worse. You are tempted to give up trying to be kind or honest, since it seems pointless.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Give up; one person's goodness cannot change anything.
Become cynical, so you are never disappointed again.
Stop reading news entirely and ignore the world's problems.
Keep choosing goodness with hope, trusting that what is right is always renewed.
apply.why: In 4.7 and 4.8 Krishna promises that whenever righteousness declines, he comes to protect the good and re-establish what is right.

lessons.reflect: Where have I seen goodness quietly return, even after hard times?
lessons.practice: Do one small act of kindness today as a vote for the goodness you hope to see.

lessons.title: Act without being stained
lessons.teaching: People approach the Divine in many ways, and each is met in their own way. Krishna acts in the world but is not stained by his actions because he does not crave their results. The wise of old understood this and kept doing their work, and we can too.
lessons.keyIdea: Craving results binds; free action does not.

apply.scenario: You volunteer at a food bank, but you have started feeling bitter because nobody thanks you or notices how much you do.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Keep serving, and let go of the need for thanks, so the work stays light and free.
Quit, since unappreciated work is not worth your time.
Post about your volunteering so people finally recognize you.
Do less until someone notices and appreciates you.
apply.why: In 4.14 Krishna says actions do not bind him because he has no craving for their fruits, and that knowing this frees us too.

lessons.reflect: Which of my good actions have quietly become a way of asking for recognition?
lessons.practice: Do one helpful thing today that nobody will ever find out about.

lessons.title: Calm inside, busy outside
lessons.teaching: Even wise people find it hard to know what true action and inaction are. Krishna says the wise can be calm inside while busy outside. When we let go of attachment to results and stay content, our work no longer weighs on us.
lessons.keyIdea: Be fully busy, and still be at rest inside.

apply.scenario: You are a new parent juggling work and a baby. You feel you can only find peace once life slows down, months or years from now.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Put peace on hold; it is only possible once life is quieter.
Cut back on caring for the baby so you can relax more.
Stay engaged in your duties while letting go of clinging, so peace is found within the busyness.
Push yourself harder to finish everything so you can rest later.
apply.why: In 4.18 Krishna says the wise see inaction in action, and in 4.20 that one who is content and unattached is free even while fully engaged.

lessons.reflect: What would it feel like to be at peace in the middle of my busiest day?
lessons.practice: During one busy task today, pause for one breath and notice the stillness under the activity.

lessons.title: Steady in success and failure
lessons.teaching: A person who is content with what comes, free of envy and even-minded in success and failure, can act without being bound. When work is done as an offering, it leaves no heavy trace. Seen this way, everything, even everyday tasks, becomes sacred.
lessons.keyIdea: Win or lose, keep your center.

apply.scenario: A colleague got the promotion you wanted. You feel envious and keep comparing your achievements to theirs all week.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Look for flaws in their work to prove you deserved it more.
Pretend you are fine while quietly resenting them.
Decide never to try for promotions again so you do not get hurt.
Notice the envy, let it go, and stay steady in your own work whether you win or lose.
apply.why: In 4.22 Krishna describes the free person as content, free from envy, and even-minded in success and failure.

lessons.reflect: How might my week feel if my peace did not depend on how I compare to others?
lessons.practice: Congratulate someone sincerely today on a success you wish had been yours.

lessons.title: Many ways to give
lessons.teaching: Krishna describes many kinds of yajna (offering): giving wealth, practicing self-discipline, studying, eating moderately, even breathing with awareness. There is no single right way to give. When life becomes an offering, it gains a deep sweetness.
lessons.keyIdea: Any part of life can become an offering.

apply.scenario: You want to contribute to your community, but you have little money to donate and feel you have nothing worthwhile to give.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Wait until you earn more, since money is the only real way to give.
Offer what you do have, like time, skills or care, since there are many ways to give.
Feel guilty and stay away from community events for now.
Give only when someone directly asks you for help.
apply.why: In 4.28 Krishna says some offer wealth, some discipline and some study, showing that offerings take many forms.

lessons.reflect: What do I have, besides money, that I could offer to others?
lessons.practice: Offer one skill or one hour of your time to someone who could use it this week.

lessons.title: Learn humbly, see the whole
lessons.teaching: The offering of wisdom is greater than offering things, because all action finds its fulfilment in understanding. Krishna says to learn from those who know, with humility, questions and service. This wisdom helps us see all beings as connected, and no past mistake is beyond its reach.
lessons.keyIdea: Humble questions open the door to wisdom.

apply.scenario: You have just joined a new team. A senior colleague knows a lot, but asking feels embarrassing, so you keep struggling silently on your own.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Keep struggling alone so no one thinks you are weak.
Pretend you already know and figure it out later.
Approach them humbly, ask sincere questions, and offer help where you can.
Wait for them to notice you are struggling and offer help first.
apply.why: In 4.34 Krishna says to learn from the wise through humility, sincere questions and service.

lessons.reflect: What am I too proud or shy to ask about, and who could help me learn it?
lessons.practice: Ask one sincere question today to someone who knows more than you about something.

lessons.title: Cut through doubt and rise
lessons.teaching: Nothing purifies like real understanding, and it grows through sincere trust and steady practice. Endless doubt leaves us stuck and unhappy. Krishna urges Arjuna to cut through the doubt in his heart with wisdom and rise to act.
lessons.keyIdea: Let wisdom cut through doubt, then stand up and act.

apply.scenario: You have wanted to start learning music for years, but you keep doubting whether you are talented enough, so you never begin.
apply.question: What would the Gita suggest?
options: Look honestly at the doubt, trust the path, and take the first step today.
Wait until you are completely sure you will be good at it.
Ask everyone you know if they think you have talent first.
Give up the idea, since doubt means it is not meant for you.
apply.why: In 4.42 Krishna tells Arjuna to cut through doubt with the sword of wisdom and rise, and 4.40 notes constant doubt brings no happiness.

lessons.reflect: Which doubt has been holding me back the longest, and is it really true?
lessons.practice: Take one small first step today on something you have been doubting yourself about.
